title: Communicate product ideas faster, with less cognitive load

content:
For most of my career, the hard part of product management was building. Every feature cost weeks of engineering time, so a lot of our work went into making sure we built the right thing. We wrote documents, added screenshots and annotated mockups, and in some companies built clickable prototypes in Figma. All of it existed to avoid wasting scarce engineering capacity.

AI has changed that equation. A working prototype can exist the afternoon an idea comes up. Engineers, designers and product managers use coding agents to turn a description into working software in hours. Teams ship more, and they ship more often.

What has not changed is human attention. Customers, account managers, support teams and leadership have the same hours in the day as before. They can only absorb so many changes, review so many ideas and give feedback on so many solutions. That attention is now the bottleneck in product management.

More output, same attention

When building is cheap, it is tempting to ship everything. The backlog shrinks, the release notes grow and the team feels productive. But every change asks something of someone. Customers have to notice it, learn it and trust it. Showering them with features leads to a chaotic experience: interfaces that keep shifting, settings that move and updates nobody reads. At some point customers stop noticing what is new, and good work disappears in the noise.

In B2B, the same applies internally. Account managers, customer success and support teams have to understand a change before a customer asks about it. They need to know what changed, who it affects and how to explain it. When a key account calls about a feature the account manager has never seen, trust suffers on both sides. Hand-written release notes and a monthly enablement session cannot keep pace with a team that ships every day.

Feedback suffers too. To know which solutions deserve a place in the product, you need customer input. But customers did not sign up to test your ideas. Every survey, interview request and beta invite competes for the same limited time, and the more you ask, the less you get back.

Spend attention on fewer things

The first response is to decide better. AI can generate options and even rank them, but it does not carry responsibility for the outcome. People set the priorities, and those decisions rest on what humans understand and care about: the customer's context, the company's strategy and the trade-offs a team is willing to make.

This makes prioritisation the core of the job again. The more a team can build, the more its value lies in what it chooses not to ship. A clear product strategy, a small number of outcomes per quarter and the discipline to say no protect both the customer experience and the attention of the people around the product.

It also changes what a good roadmap looks like. Instead of a list of features, it becomes a short list of problems worth customers' and colleagues' attention.

Make every message cheaper to absorb

The second response is to change how we communicate. People judge an experience much faster than a description. A paragraph in a spec asks the reader to imagine the product; a prototype lets them use it. A clickable prototype gets clearer feedback in five minutes than a document does in a week.

The same applies to internal communication. A two-minute narrated demo per release lets account managers and support catch up between calls, and gives them something to forward to customers. Generated from the same scripts the team uses for testing, it stays in sync with the product without extra work.

Showing is now cheap enough to be the default. A demo is still not evidence, though. A polished prototype can win a room without having been tested with a single customer. It starts a conversation with customers; it does not replace one.

What this means for the product operating model

Marty Cagan's product operating model, described in Transformed, covers three dimensions: deciding which problems to solve, discovering solutions and delivering them. For years, most effort and most process went into delivery, because that was where the cost was.

AI has accelerated discovery and delivery. That puts more weight on the first dimension, and on the communication that connects all three. Deciding which problems deserve attention, and making solutions easy for others to understand, is where product leaders now add most value. Empowered teams also earn trust by showing their work, and that has never been easier.

This is part 1 of the series The Bottleneck is moving. Part 2 covers communication within and between teams, part 3 how to let everyone in your company prototype, and part 4 automated demo videos with Claude, Playwright and HeyGen. If you see this playing out differently in your team, I would like to hear about it.
